title: Morning Edition
dek: Russia's latest barrage underscores the civilian cost of the Ukraine war; India joins the rate-tightening cycle; an imported Ebola case tests border surveillance; and a neighborhood pumpkin wall offers a smaller measure of the world.

lead_story.headline: Russia's overnight barrage kills civilians across Ukraine, with nine dead in one Pryluky apartment strike
lead_story.summary: Russia launched a large missile-and-drone attack across Ukraine early Wednesday. In Pryluky, a missile hit a residential building; Ukrainian police reported nine dead there, including three children, while strikes elsewhere caused additional deaths, injuries and power disruptions.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The attack shows the continuing civilian and infrastructure cost of the war and the particular difficulty Ukraine faces against ballistic missiles even as its drone interception improves.

items.headline: India raises interest rates for the first time in nearly four years
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India raised its repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% and shifted to a calibrated-tightening stance as inflation pressures from energy, food and global financial conditions increased.
items.why_it_matters: India had been an important holdout from the renewed global tightening cycle. The move raises borrowing costs in one of the world's fastest-growing major economies while showing how the energy shock is spreading into domestic monetary policy.

items.headline: Kenya's first imported Bundibugyo Ebola case exposes the limits of border screening
items.summary: Kenya confirmed that a citizen infected during the major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda and flew to Nairobi before dying. Authorities are tracing contacts and strengthening surveillance.
items.why_it_matters: The case is a practical test of cross-border outbreak control: symptom checks and travel declarations can reduce risk, but they are imperfect when disease moves through ordinary transport networks.

items.headline: Brazil is heading to a Lula–Flávio Bolsonaro runoff after an unusually close first round
items.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro finished the first round with 47.03% of valid votes and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva with 45.16%, sending the presidential contest to an October 25 runoff.
items.why_it_matters: The result leaves Latin America's largest democracy with a genuinely competitive second round whose outcome will affect fiscal policy, environmental policy, public security and Brazil's external alignment.

items.headline: A quieter geopolitical contest is forming around the minerals modern economies require
items.summary: A Reuters analysis traces competition over copper, lithium, rare earths and other strategic materials from Balochistan and Central Asia to new recovery and extraction efforts in Japan, South Korea and the United States.
items.why_it_matters: Energy systems, data centers, electronics and defense supply chains all depend on material inputs that are geographically concentrated. Resource security is increasingly shaping alliances and industrial policy away from the most visible wars.

items.headline: A Charlotte neighborhood is preparing its 22nd wall of glowing jack-o'-lanterns
items.summary: Residents of the Elizabeth neighborhood will again build a roughly 20-foot community wall filled with carved pumpkins, with neighbors carving together before the October 25 lighting and the pumpkins composted afterward.
items.why_it_matters: It is exactly the sort of ordinary civic ritual that rarely enters a national news feed: neighbors repeatedly making a place feel like their place.

items.headline: Science's knowledge problem is not producing studies; it is assembling what they collectively mean
items.summary: Nature editor Helen Pearson argues that individual studies are routinely overinterpreted and that systematic evidence synthesis is an essential, underappreciated part of science. The problem becomes more urgent as AI makes both research production and low-quality review production easier.
items.why_it_matters: It offers a useful rule for reading science—and for using AI to understand it: a new result matters less in isolation than in relation to the whole body of evidence.

worth_your_time.headline: The Work
worth_your_time.summary: Katherine Cusumano follows independent professional wrestlers through the Pacific Northwest circuit, focusing less on celebrity wrestling than on the labor, choreography, personas and stubborn ambition required to keep performing.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: The piece uses a deliberately artificial form of entertainment to examine something real: how people build identities, communities and meaningful work around a craft that outsiders can easily dismiss.

worth_your_time.headline: Eating Alone
worth_your_time.summary: Gabe Bullard examines what food delivery, ghost kitchens and app-mediated convenience have changed about restaurants and eating, arguing that frictionless digital services often push complexity into the physical world rather than eliminating it.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: It is a concrete way into a broader question about convenience: when we remove effort from an individual transaction, what social spaces, labor and shared habits are quietly redesigned to make that possible?
